profile.campus: Ashburn, Loudoun County, Virginia (Equinix Ashburn campus, Data Center Alley)
profile.reading:
This building operates as Equinix's DC10 data center at 21551 Beaumeade Circle in Ashburn, Virginia, one node in Equinix's cluster of buildings spread across Loudoun County's Data Center Alley, sited on Beaumeade Circle alongside Equinix's DC22 building tracked elsewhere in this registry rather than on the Filigree Court cluster nearby. Equinix's own DC10 facility page publishes concrete numbers rather than general marketing text, 84,830 square feet of space, N+1 generator redundancy rated for 30 hours or more at full load, N+1 cooling redundancy, seismic category A construction under the 2006 Universal Building Code, a one story reinforced concrete building with a raised floor rated at 8,354 psf, and ten compliance certifications including LEED alongside HECVAT, HIPAA, ISO 9001, ISO 22301, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53/FISMA High, PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, and SOC 2 Type II. LEED certification is a fact Equinix confirms for DC10 that does not appear on the DC1, DC3, or DC5 pages nearby on this same campus. Equinix's page does not display a UPS redundancy figure for DC10, showing a contact sales placeholder in that field, and Equinix does not publish an IT load or utility power figure in megawatts for DC10 itself, so this entry does not assign one.

Ashburn's status as the center of Data Center Alley predates Equinix's arrival. AOL built what is generally regarded as the area's first data center, its Dulles Technology Center, in 1997 to support its dial up internet subscriber base, and the fiber capacity that project pulled into Loudoun County helped seed the cluster of interconnected facilities that followed. Equinix opened its own first Ashburn building, DC1, in the late 1990s, and its second building, DC2, earned a reputation, per Data Center Dynamics, as one of the most connected buildings on earth. Loudoun County's data center corridor has since grown into what Data Center Dynamics describes as roughly 10 million square feet of built space consuming on the order of 1 gigawatt of electrical power region wide, a figure covering every operator in the corridor rather than Equinix alone.

Equinix's own Washington D.C. metro listing page currently names and links 15 facilities together, DC1 through DC6, DC10 through DC16, DC21, and DC22, with most addresses in Ashburn and at least one, DC14, in nearby Manassas. Equinix does not publish a combined power or square footage total for that group of buildings, and Equinix markets DC10 through DC12 alongside DC1 through DC6 collectively as offering access to one of the top three internet peering exchange markets on the East Coast, without singling out DC10's own peering density or customer roster.

Every data center on this campus now also sits inside Virginia's evolving electricity regulatory framework for large power users. The State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates in November 2026 that raise a typical residential bill by about 16 dollars a month, while creating a new GS-5 rate class specifically for data centers, effective January 1, 2027, that requires large demand customers like Equinix's Ashburn buildings to sign 14 year minimum contracts with cost coverage guarantees, according to Inside Climate News's reporting on the commission's decision.

reading.body:
DC10 is an 84,830 square foot building on Beaumeade Circle in Ashburn, Virginia, part of Equinix's 15-facility cluster spanning Loudoun County. The facility publishes N+1 generator redundancy rated for 30 hours or more at full load, N+1 cooling redundancy, and seismic category A construction, but Equinix does not publish a utility power capacity in megawatts for DC10 itself. The building holds ten compliance certifications including LEED, HIPAA, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53/FISMA High, PCI DSS, and SOC 2 Type II, which qualify it to host regulated workloads in healthcare, finance, and government, and to serve customers requiring high-assurance security postures.

Ashburn's Data Center Alley, anchored by AOL's 1997 Dulles Technology Center and Equinix's own late-1990s DC1 and DC2 buildings, is described as the greatest concentration of data center space on the planet at roughly 10 million square feet across all operators in the corridor consuming on the order of 1 gigawatt of power. Equinix markets DC10 through DC12 alongside DC1 through DC6 collectively as offering access to one of the top three internet peering exchange markets on the US East Coast, though Equinix does not publish peering density or customer roster for DC10 separately. Virginia's State Corporation Commission approved new Dominion Energy rates effective January 2027 that create a GS-5 rate class requiring large data center operators like Equinix to sign 14 year minimum contracts with cost coverage guarantees, binding the economics of this and every other facility on the campus to a long-term regulatory commitment.

In Virginia, 330 facilities are mapped in public records, only 25 publish power capacity figures, and the state's total published capacity is 1,603 megawatts across all operators. Equinix's Ashburn campus ranks 26th by published megawatts in the state, but Equinix does not publish a combined power figure for its 15 linked buildings in the D.C. metro area, so the actual power scale of the cluster at this location remains opaque relative to what Equinix discloses at other campuses.
